entries.topicDescription: Safely handling the absence of a value in Swift.

tips.title: Prefer if-let and guard-let over force unwrapping
tips.content:
Optionals in Swift represent a value that may or may not exist.
Force unwrapping with '!' crashes your app if the value is nil.

Use 'if let' to safely unwrap an optional into a local constant
that is only available inside the if-block. This guarantees you
never access a nil value.

Use 'guard let' when you want to exit early. It unwraps the
optional and makes the value available for the rest of the scope.
This keeps your code flat and readable — no deep nesting.

As a rule of thumb, use guard-let in functions where a nil value
means you cannot proceed, and if-let when you want to do
something optional with the value.

tips.title: Use nil-coalescing and optional chaining together
tips.content:
The nil-coalescing operator '??' provides a default value when
an optional is nil. It reads naturally: "use this value, or
fall back to that."

Optional chaining with '?.' lets you call methods or access
properties on an optional without unwrapping it first. If any
link in the chain is nil, the entire expression returns nil.

Combining both is extremely powerful. You can chain through
deeply nested optional properties and provide a sensible
default at the end, all in one readable expression.

This avoids nested if-let pyramids and makes your intent
crystal clear to other developers reading your code.

tips.title: Map and flatMap on optionals
tips.content:
Optionals in Swift conform to a pattern similar to functional
containers. You can call 'map' on an optional to transform its
wrapped value without unwrapping it manually.

If the optional is nil, map returns nil. If it has a value,
map applies your closure and wraps the result back in an optional.

Use 'flatMap' when your transformation itself returns an optional.
'map' would give you a double-optional (String??), while flatMap
flattens it into a single optional (String?).

This functional style removes boilerplate if-let blocks and
makes chains of transformations concise and expressive.
